fatal_errors: The proposed material is a generic CoCrFeNiMo-type laser-clad FCC/σ coating rather than the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 L12/B2 lamellar eutectic alloy in the target study.

The suggested aqueous 3.5 wt.% NaCl tribocorrosion test at approximately 600 °C is not physically defined under ordinary test-cell conditions because liquid water cannot be maintained there without a specialized high-pressure system.
The proposed comparison omits the identically conditioned duplex stainless steel 2205 baseline and the rapid heating/quenching treatment to approximately 1100 °C.

It attributes degradation primarily to interphase microgalvanic corrosion, whereas the target mechanism is the temperature-dependent competition among depassivation, repassivation, tribolayer stability, abrasion, and oxide-layer fracture.

It predicts that the multiphase HEA degrades more than a single-phase baseline, missing the observed superior wear, friction, passivation, and structural stability of the eutectic HEA relative to DS2205.

Compositional tuning cannot simultaneously produce a single-phase comparator and preserve the same nominal composition; heat treatment may also alter grain size, precipitates, hardness, and residual stress, confounding phase-count effects.
explanation: The response recognizes a broadly relevant wear–film-rupture–corrosion feedback and offers a nominally testable multiphase-versus-single-phase comparison. However, it reconstructs neither the actual alloy system nor the comparator, conditioning, temperature range, aqueous environment, or observed nonmonotonic temperature response. The limited overlap is repeated passive-film rupture and oxidative or third-body damage at high temperature. Evidence E1 supports a generic tradeoff in which multiphase CoCrFeNiMo coatings can have better wear resistance but poorer corrosion resistance, but it does not establish simultaneous tribocorrosion, a 600 °C aqueous mechanism, or applicability to L12/B2 AlCoCrFeNi2.1. E2 and E3 concern different compositions and separate corrosion or wear measurements and do not validate the claimed coupled mechanism. The falsification test has some discriminating value, but its proposed comparator is strongly confounded and the rule does not require direct evidence of phase-selective attack or galvanic current. A valid test would need feasible matched conditions, independent wear/corrosion decomposition, and direct interphase electrochemical or localized-attack measurements.
